title: Electrical engineering
note: Ohm's law V = IR links voltage, current, and resistance, and power is P = VI. Kirchhoff's current law (charge conservation): currents into a node equal currents out. Kirchhoff's voltage law (energy conservation): voltages around any closed loop sum to zero. Capacitors store energy in electric fields, inductors in magnetic fields.

read.title: Two rules for every circuit
text: Electrical engineering starts with three quantities. Voltage is the energy per charge that pushes current; current is the rate at which charge flows; resistance opposes that flow. Ohm's law ties them together as V = IR, and the power a component uses is P = VI.

Two rules from Gustav Kirchhoff let you analyze any network of components. The current law says that charge does not pile up at a junction, so the current flowing in equals the current flowing out. The voltage law says that if you walk around any closed loop and add every rise and drop in voltage, you return to zero, because energy is conserved. With these rules, a circuit becomes a set of equations.

Not every component is a resistor. A capacitor stores energy in the electric field between its plates and blocks steady DC once charged. An inductor stores energy in a magnetic field and resists sudden changes in current. A diode lets current pass mainly in one direction, and a transistor lets a small signal control a large current, which makes amplifiers and the logic gates of every computer possible.
Power grids use AC because transformers can raise the voltage for long lines, cutting current and I²R losses, then lower it again for homes.
